Items.Authors: Paul Hickson, Kuntal Misra, Jean Surdej, Bhavya Ailawadhi, Monalisa Dubey, Naveen Dukiya, Priyanshi Kumari, Gokul Singh Mehra, Vibhore Negi, Anna Pospieszalska-Surdej, Kumar Pranshu, Sarvesh Kumar Yadav
Items.Title: Performance of the International Liquid Mirror Telescope
Items.Abstract: The International Liquid Mirror Telescope (ILMT) is a 4-meter zenith-pointing astronomical survey telescope. Located at Devasthal Peak in the Indian Himalayas, the project is a collaboration between institutions in Belgium, India and Canada. Its primary scientific program is the detection and study of transient and variable sources. A unique feature of the ILMT is its primary mirror which employs liquid mercury as the reflecting surface. Equipped with a 4096 x 4096 pixel CCD camera, the telescope records images of a 22.4 arcmin wide strip of sky passing overhead, revisiting every object in the strip each night for several months. The ILMT began operation in 2022, and has now obtained over 1900 hours of imaging data. We provide an overview of the project and discuss the performance of the telescope, including image quality, limiting magnitudes, observing statistics, data products and the transient detection success rate.

Items.Authors: Romain Laugier, Lucas Labadie, Denis Defrère, Marc-Antoine Martinod, Guillermo Martin
Items.Title: Phase-sensing with the modified Mach-Zehnder nuller
Items.Abstract: Integrated-optics tricouplers are one of the rare nulling beam-combiners that can provide phase sensing in operation, but they lack a bulk optics equivalent.  With this work, we demonstrate how this sensing ability arises in the beam combination, and how it fundamentally comes at the cost of off-axis light. We then propose a novel alteration to the modified Mach-Zehnder topology (Serabyn 2001) of balanced beamsplitter to bring sensing capabilities by recycling light already shed by the combiner to balance intensity at no additional throughput cost. This new option offers a pivotal new architecture options for fine piston control accuracy and null maintenance with reduced overheads.

Items.Authors: Hirofumi Okita, Naoyuki Tamura, Takashi Hattori, Yuhei Takagi, Yusei Koyama, Masayuki Kuzuhara, Hatsune Uekiyo
Items.Title: PI-type instrumentation at the Subaru Telescope
Items.Abstract: We explain the PI-type Instrumentation program at the Subaru Telescope. The Subaru Telescope has a framework for PI-type instruments, which are developed, assembled, integrated, tested, and operated using external funding and human resources to achieve specific science goals or demonstrate novel technology, and which complement with facility instruments that are developed, maintained, and operated by resources of the Subaru Telescope. In this paper, we briefly explain outline and uniqueness of the PI-type instrumentation program at the Subaru Telescope, as well as the brief summary of the approval process of the PI-type instruments and current problems. We will also summarize the results of the productivity study and user opinions survey discussed at the PI-type instrument workshop held in October 2025.

Items.Authors: Jaya Chand
Items.Title: Polaris and Zenith non-tracking Differential Image Motion Monitors for robust atmospheric turbulence monitoring
Items.Abstract: Traditional DIMM seeing monitors depend on bright stars and accurate tracking mounts, increasing system cost, complexity, and maintenance.To address this, we present two wide-field, static, untracked DIMMs: the Polaris DIMM and the Zenith DIMM.These instruments aim to provide reliable Fried parameter measurements with minimal infrastructure and autonomous operation.The Polaris DIMM continuously observes Polaris without tracking but cannot operate in equatorial regions or the southern hemisphere.To achieve global applicability, the Zenith DIMM uses an even larger field of view with fixed pointing to function at any latitude.Both prototypes were installed on the ING DIMM tower at ORM, La Palma, where they showed good agreement with the ING robotic DIMM (R2D2).Using scintillation index and covariance, we also estimate a simple three-layer turbulence profile, from which the isoplanatic angle, and with wind information, the coherence time and photometric scintillation noise, can be derived.

Items.Authors: Federico Astori
Items.Title: POLOCALC and HoverCal drone system: attitude reconstruction software
Items.Abstract: Precise calibration of the absolute polarization angle is critical for detecting primordial B-mode signals in the cosmic microwave background. The POLOCALC and HoverCal projects operate drone-borne polarized microwave emitters (90–280 GHz) to provide a stable far-field reference for telescopes. The key innovation is the use of photogrammetry, tightly integrated with onboard sensors, to determine the drone’s attitude with extreme precision, directly linking the orientation of the emitted polarization signal to fixed ground references. Leveraging this technique, the system aims to achieve absolute polarization angle calibration with an accuracy of σΨ ~ 0.01°, sufficient for searching primordial B-modes at the level σ_r ~ 10⁻³. Photogrammetry is central to determining the polarization plane’s orientation in celestial coordinates, employing a sophisticated color-filtering algorithm and a Bayesian framework to retrieve the drone’s attitude within these stringent accuracy requirements.

Items.Authors: Vincenzo Cotroneo, Giovanni Pareschi, Stefano Basso, Marta M. Civitani, Thorsten Dohring, Eugenio Gibertini, Giorgia Sironi, Daniele Spiga
Items.Title: Polydopamine overcoatings for soft X-ray reflectivity enhancements: recent progress and performance assessment
Items.Abstract: We present recent advances in dopamine-based overcoatings to enhance the soft X-ray performance of grazing-incidence telescope mirrors. Thin polydopamine (PDA) films, deposited by dip-coating from aqueous solution, provide a carbon-rich, low-density layer on conventional high-Z coatings (e.g. Au, Ir, Ir/Cr), offering an attractive, lower-cost alternative to sputtered carbon or other carbon-based films (e.g. SiC, B₄C). We report an expanded set of laboratory and synchrotron reflectivity measurements, together with process optimization (thickness control, uniformity, reproducibility), tests on relevant mirror geometries, and an assessment of surface roughness and small-angle scattering. Ongoing environmental and adhesion studies, combined with updated optical modelling, support the potential application of these coatings in future cost-constrained spaceborne X-ray telescopes requiring large effective area in the soft band.

Items.Authors: Michael Mann, Thorsten Döhring, Alessandro Priebsch, Udo Sauer, Alexander Stock, Georgios Fotis
Items.Title: Power quality diagnostics at astronomical observatories
Items.Abstract: Astronomical observatories supplied by long radial grids are highly susceptible to power quality disturbances. Conventional monitoring based on 10‑minute RMS aggregation systematically suppresses fast transient and subtransient phenomena, although these directly affect electromagnetic compatibility and measurement stability.  This work introduces a diagnostic methodology using transient recorders for synchronized, microsecond‑resolution measurements of voltage and current across phase, neutral, and protective earth conductors. The approach combines time‑domain analysis with frequency‑dependent impedance characterization.  Experimental results show that fast events with significant amplitudes occur and are governed by grid impedance, while remaining invisible in standardized PQ metrics. The methodology provides a physically interpretable extension of conventional power quality assessment for weak and inverter‑dominated systems.

Items.Authors: Carlos M. Correia, Kyliann Robert, Cyril Petit, Jean-Marc Conan
Items.Title: Predictive atmospheric models for servo-lag mitigation in frozen-flow-dominated regimes: application to free space communications and high-contrast imagers
Items.Abstract: Adaptive Optics systems in Free-Space Optics (FSO) links and High Contrast Imaging are strongly limited by the system's servo-lag error. This work evaluates auto-regressive (AR) models that exploit the measurable temporal correlation in wavefront distortions to predict future turbulence states and enable to compensate for the system latency. A fully analytic framework is developed to estimate the residual error variance and determine the optimal AR order and prediction horizon under varying turbulence conditions and sampling rates. Experiments on ONERA’s PICOLO and LISA benches are presented where we tested the theoretical expectations. Results show in these high wind speed regimes large Strehl Ratio gains and improved FSO link stability.

Items.Authors: Aya Harkat, Henri-François Raynaud, Nicolas Galland, Arthur Vigan, Axel Potier, Mamadou N’Diaye, Kjetil Dohlen, Caroline Kulcsár
Items.Title: Predictive control for the compensation of NCPAs measured with SPHERE/ZELDA
Items.Abstract: This work presents a predictive LQG control strategy to mitigate non-common path aberrations (NCPAs) in high-contrast imaging instruments for exoplanet detection. Using experimental post-AO data from the SPHERE/ZELDA sensor at 0.5 Hz, auto-regressive (AR) disturbance models are identified for 860 Zernike modes, leading to as many independent LQG regulators operating in parallel.     The performance of the global controller is evaluated through the RMS and peak-to-valley of the residuals, showing improved compensation compared with a standard well-tuned modal.

Items.Authors: Ludo Bissot, Florian Quatresooz, Gilles Orban de Xivry, Baptiste Delvaux, Olivier Absil, Claude Oestges
Items.Title: Predictive control of atmospheric turbulence for optical ground stations
Items.Abstract: Atmospheric turbulence degrades satellite to ground optical links, especially under poor conditions and fast low-Earth-orbit tracking. To reduce the temporal error, the principal limitation in such scenarios, we investigate predictive control for adaptive optics within the SALTO telescope, a Belgian test platform for compact optical communication systems. Turbulence statistics at the Redu Space Center are derived from Weather Research and Forecasting simulations. Three controllers are compared: an LQG regulator based on an AR(1) turbulence model, a LQG VAR(2) and a linear data-driven Empirical Orthogonal Functions (EOF) predictor.

Items.Authors: Lingling Wang, Jinqing Wang
Items.Title: Preliminary: Signal path variation induced by structural deformation in large radio telescopes
Items.Abstract: Variations in the signal path of a radio telescope are a critical factor affecting observation accuracy, with path changes induced by structural deformation serving as a primary error source. This presentation will systematically overview the authors’ latest research on how structural deformation impacts telescope signal path variations, emphasizing the validation of relevant models through a combination of measurements, simulations, and theoretical calculations.

Items.Authors: Jorge Parra, Mario Castro
Items.Title: Prioritizing maintenance workforce effort in ground-based telescopes through a risk-based maintenance strategy
Items.Abstract: Optimizing astronomical observatory uptime requires a prioritized, proactive maintenance approach. This paper proposes a Risk-Based Maintenance (RBM) framework to strategically allocate maintenance workforce and operational windows for ground-based telescopes. The methodology systematically identifies critical systems, assesses failure possibility and operational consequences, and incorporates current equipment status to calculate a comprehensive risk score. This score objectively ranks maintenance tasks, directing limited resources to the most critical components. This data-driven prioritization replaces traditional time-based or reactive methods, boosting telescope reliability and longevity. The discussion will cover RBM model development, integration with a Computerized Maintenance Management System (CMMS), and expected benefits, including reduced downtime, optimized labor use, and maintenance standardization.

Items.Authors: Florian Kerber, Raul Cordero, Omar Cuevas, Susana Deustua, Patricio Galeas, Markus Gaug, Rory Gillespie, Miska Le Louarn, Julio C. Marin, Ricardo C. Munoz, Angel Otarola, Anna Francesca Pala, Jérôme Paufique, Joseph P. Rice, Roberto Rondanelli, Alain Smette, Roberta Zanin
Items.Title: Profiling of the Atmosphere by Remote Sensing and Radiosonde Balloon Launches above our Astronomical Observatory Sites - PARABOLAS
Items.Abstract: The European Southern Observatory (ESO) is teaming up with international partners to conduct a measurement campaign with the main objective of characterizing a significant volume of atmosphere above the Paranal (VLT), Armazones (ELT) and the future Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO) South sites covering a horizontal distance of about 25 km between the observatory sites and an altitude of at least 15 km to address both its spatial and temporal variations using an array of in-situ and remote sensing instrumentation. The campaign’s results will be key for the science operations of ESO’s fully adaptive Extremely Large Telescope, and highly relevant for the NIST Stars project on Paranal, and for the CTAO which uses the atmosphere as its detection medium for gamma rays. The campaign is currently scheduled for 2026/27. We’ll report on the current status of planning and the next steps towards the actual implementation.

Items.Authors: Xiaoyun Ma, Ruirui Fan, Wei Wang, Nannan Yue, Xiangxiang Ren, Xaojing Wu, Yu Wang, Yuxin Qiu, Fei Liu, Hanzhang Wang, Ran Duan
Items.Title: Progress on a scalable FPGA-GPU heterogeneous 10k-Pixel TES/MKID readout
Items.Abstract: Although current frequency-division multiplexing umux TES/MKID readouts can achieve multiplexing ratios of thousands of pixels on a single signal line, large arrays of 10k or even 100k pixels still require multiple readout units. This work presents a 10k-pixels readout system implemented on an FPGA-GPU heterogeneous architecture. The FPGA handles the shared signal processing algorithms for both TES and MKID, while the GPU manages the remaining demodulation steps specific to each detector. This approach supports both detector types and facilitates development and debugging. This paper will also discuss the design and challenges of multi-unit systems within the heterogeneous architecture.

Items.Authors: P. Dal Bo, M. Pinchera, D. Calabro, J. Cliche, G. Coppi, S. Della Torre, G. Delle Monache, M. De Lucia, E. Di Giorgi, M. Dobbs, T. Lari, K. Leonova, A. Limonta, M. Massa, A. Moggi, J. Montgomery, D. Nicolò, A. Novelli, A. Passerini, L. Porcelli, M. Rossella, G. Smecher, A. Tartari, F. Tramonti, L. Zanga, M. Zannoni, G. Signorelli
Items.Title: Progress on the path towards the TRL-6 qualification of the LiteBIRD SQUID controller unit
Items.Abstract: LiteBIRD is a JAXA-led satellite mission planned for the 2030s to measure CMB polarization and search for the faint B-mode signal of inflation. Detecting this signal requires ultra-low-noise, polarization-sensitive TES bolometers read out with digital frequency-division multiplexing using LC filters and SQUID amplifiers. The warm electronics include the Signal-Processing Assembly, Digitizer Assembly, and the SQUID Controller Assembly (SCA), which provides SQUID biasing and preamplification for four channels. INFN is responsible for designing and space-qualifying the SQUID Controller Unit (SCU), which integrates eight SCAs in a dedicated enclosure with mechanical support, thermal interface, and EMI shielding. This work reports the SCU qualification toward TRL6, including thermal-vacuum environmental tests on an SCU setup with one active SCA and seven dummies.

Items.Authors: Raveena Khan, M. S. Savitha, K. Nagaraju
Items.Title: Prototype development of a visible-light polarimeter: a path to EUV spectropolarimetry
Items.Abstract: Scientists are working to unlock the Sun’s magnetic secrets by studying how light is polarized in different wavelengths. Earlier experiments with the SOHO satellite showed the technique of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) polarization measurement could reveal magnetic fields in the Sun’s corona, but progress has been limited by the lack of sensitive polarimetric instruments. To address this, we have designed and built a polarimeter prototype using three mirrors arranged in a special design. Tested with aluminum mirrors at visible light, the reflection-based polarimeter shows verified results. Future versions will operate in the EUV range, paving the way for direct measurements of coronal magnetic fields.

Items.Authors: Thibaut Prod'Homme, Carlos Corral Van Damme, Timo Rühl, Kate Isaak, Marco Sirianni, Jens Loehring, Massimo Lucia, Massimo Falcolini, Jean-Philippe Halain, Luc Boucher, Peter Verhoeve, Eloy Hernandez, Laurence Soulat, Marc Broussely, Matthew Vaughan, Albertus Kusumo Adi, Diego Escorial Olmos, Rafael Guzmán, Santiago Serrano, Stefan Kögl, Florian Kehl, Antonio Rodríguez-Senín, Paola Kögl, Eider Ocerin, David Mateo, Juan Oñate, Eduardo Ugalde, Marcos Ubierna, Aitor Barrena, Laura Burgos, Marco Truglio, Iñigo Ojanguren, Ignacio Torralbo, Leire Benito, Yasin Tahiri, Dan Tye, Hans-Peter Gröbelbauer, Florian Wirz, Gerhard Székely, Eloi Vázquez Codesido, Clément Charuel, Etienne Lallemand, Jean-Yves Plesseria, Gabriel Giono, Harald Ottacher
Items.Title: Prototyping ARRAKIHS: accelerating and derisking instrument development for an ESA fast-class mission
Items.Abstract: Fast-class missions in ESA’s science programme have as their main objective to nearly halve their development time compared to medium or large-class missions; 8 years from selection to launch instead of 15. In the context of this accelerated scheme, the development of bespoke high-performing instruments for space missions with attractive scientific objectives is a considerable challenge.   Using the Arrakihs mission as an example we show how prototyping during the study phase helps accelerate and derisk the development of such instruments. In this contribution, we will go through the results from more than 10 different prototyping activities from optics to detectors, from electronic boards to mechanical parts which took place during phase B and extract lessons learned.

Items.Authors: M. Faccioni, D. Kiehn, P. Vrancken
Items.Title: Quantifying the errors in modeling optical propagation in a turbulent atmosphere using different phase screen synthesization methods
Items.Abstract: In this publication, the results obtained modeling the propagation of an optical wave in a turbulent atmosphere  using three different phase screen synthesization methods are compared. The three investigated algorithms are the  classical random phase method, its optimized version adding the sub-harmonics correction, and a new method  based on the phase correlation function, called correlation-based random phase method. Their errors w.r.t.  the theoretical phase fluctuations’ structure function are computed, showing how the correlation-based random  phase method, solving the bandwidth error arising while using a single discrete Fourier transform, offers a better  accuracy w.r.t. the two other methods. Finally, the propagated waves obtained using the different methods are  compared considering their aberration content, expressed using the Zernike polynomials, and quantifying the  error committed when the phase fluctuations’ power spectral density is underestimated.

Items.Authors: Alexey V. Gorshkov, Daniel Gottesman, Emil T. Khabiboulline, Zhenning Liu, Brittany M. McClinton, Jayadev K. Rajagopal, Stephen T. Ridgway
Items.Title: Quantum-optimized phase closure for robust imaging
Items.Abstract: Closure phase enables imaging with interferometric arrays and is conventionally obtained by measuring fringe phases on individual baselines and summing them to cancel telescope-dependent phase errors. Standard measurements recover pairwise coherence terms, so the closure phase is formed in post-processing. In a quantum architecture, the optical fields are first mapped into local quantum memories and later combined through a joint measurement. Direct measurement of closure phase from the memories uses the available photons more efficiently and relaxes stability requirements. In bright scenes, a joint three-site measurement improves the Fisher information for closure-phase estimation. In the photon-starved regime, we construct observables accumulating information about the closure phase across atmospheric windows, reducing the photon requirement per window at the cost of worse visibility-amplitude scaling. We find that a quantum approach needs only three photons per stability interval.

Items.Authors: James M. Ivory, Nyasha J. Suliali, Martin J. Prest, Konstantin D. Stefanov, Jon Mason, David Hall, Manish R. Patel
Items.Title: Radiation damage in high-sensitivity, low-noise CIS120 image sensors for future space missions
Items.Abstract: This work focusses on the characterisation of the Teledyne E2v CIS120, a CMOS device planned for use in many upcoming space telescopes, with some of these interested in UV measurements.     As the main wavelengths of interest are in the UV spectrum, characterisation is primarily done on light between 200 – 400 nm, both before and after separate gamma and proton irradiations. A broad range of metrics are characterised, including dark current, noise and quantum efficiency, at room temperature, 20 °C and -25 °C.

Items.Authors: Faustine Cantalloube, Olivier Absil, Marc Van Droogenbroeck, Anthony Cioppa, Carles Cantero-Mitjans, Sébastien Piérard, Nitya Pandey
Items.Title: Ranking detection capabilities of post-processing techniques for high-contrast imaging: revisiting the Exoplanet Imaging Data Challenge phase 1
Items.Abstract: The Exoplanet Imaging Data Challenge (EIDC) is a platform that enables the high-contrast imaging (HCI) community to compare post-processing methods for different tasks, organized into different phases. In 2020 we published the results of phase 1, focused on the detection of planetary signals in data sets coming from various instruments. At the time, we used various scores to evaluate the detection performance of algorithms and provided several rankings to compare the capabilities of the 28 algorithms proposed by the 15 participants. Recently, under the impulse of the AI-based image processing community, new evaluation frameworks have emerged for ranking algorithms. Among them, the Tile is a 2-dimensional figure that displays different ranking scores for crisp two-class classifiers at a glance. In this contribution, we apply different flavors of the Tile to the results of Phase 1 of the Exoplanet Imaging Data Challenge, indicating how to analyze the performance and compare algorithms.

Items.Authors: Samantha A. Grubb
Items.Title: Ray tracing, optical modeling, and calibration of the Simons Observatory Large Aperture Telescope instrumental polarization angle
Items.Abstract: Simons Observatory (SO) is a new millimeter-wave Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) experiment located in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. SO is designed to make precise measurements of the temperature and polarization of the CMB. It has one 6 meter Large Aperture Telescope (LAT). Its receiver includes a focal plane made up of 60,000 transition-edge sensor (TES) bolometers that are sensitive to orthogonal linear polarization states. A potential scientific goal of SO is to probe for cosmic birefringence, a rotation of the CMB polarization plane that would signal new, parity-violating physics. Small miscalibrations in detector orientation and distortions from the telescope’s optics can rotate the measured CMB polarization by an instrumental angle, α, mimicking the birefringence signal. This work focuses on determining the LAT’s instrumental polarization angle using an optical model that traces rays through the telescope’s optics to determine the on-sky polarization direction.

Items.Authors: Camilo Weinberger, Elena Masciadri, Luca Carbonaro, Marlene de Sepibus, Fernando Pedichini, Ciro Del Vecchio, Christian Veillet, Sam Ragland
Items.Title: R&D activity in INAF on light instrumentation for continuous optical turbulence monitoring
Items.Abstract: Optical turbulence (OT) measurements are useful for turbulence characterization but also for the application of hybrid technics (atmospheric models plus observations) for the OT forecasts. With this in mind we started a R&D activity in INAF-Arcetri in collaboration with INAF-Rome and LBT focused on instrumentation for OT estimates. The roadmap at long time scale aims to cover different topics such as the implementation of instruments of different nature for the OT estimate, the quantification of their reliability and the development of new light instrumentation. In this work, we present an automated system designed for continuous seeing measurements during day and night using multiple sensors. The system includes a fully automatic on-site platform that monitors operational status and delivers real-time information on sensor health and measurements. Its real-time acquisition capabilities enable the generation of local datasets, and allow on-site testing for forecasting methodologies.

Items.Authors: Jialin Li, Jordan M. Stone, Kevin Wagner, Steve Ertel, Feng Long, Laird M. Close, Helene Rousseau, Virginie Faramaz, Jared Carlson, Jenny Power, Andrew Cardwell
Items.Title: Recent thermal infrared observations enabled by the NALES reduction pipeline
Items.Abstract: The Arizona Lenslets for Exoplanet Spectroscopy (ALES) is a thermal-infrared integral-field spectrograph operating within the 1–5 μm imaging camera LBTI/LMIRCam. We present a publicly available Python data-reduction pipeline for the ALES instrument, which is optimized for low-resolution (R~ 40) spectroscopy of directly imaged exoplanets and protoplanets in the 3-4 μm range. The pipeline implements the full reduction sequence, i.e., detector calibrations, lenslet spectral extraction, spectral-cube reconstruction, image selection and registration, and modular post processing for starlight subtraction. Portions of the core reduction framework build on earlier work (e.g. Stone et al. 2022, Wagner et al. 2023), which we have expanded and documented to support a broader user community and a wider range of science cases. We outline the reduction process and demonstrate its performance using on-sky observations of protoplanetary disks.

Items.Authors: David R. Andersen, Gelys Trancho, Corinne Boyer, John Miles, Lianqi Wang, Kanaka Warad, Ryuji Suzuki, Ashley Baker
Items.Title: Requirements management, performance budgeting, and traceability for the TMT first-light instruments
Items.Abstract: The TMT first-light instruments, IRIS, WFOS, and MODHIS, face demanding science goals and close integration with the observatory architecture including NFIRAOS, the facility AO system. We present the requirements management and performance budgeting framework developed to ensure scientific, functional, and interface compliance for the instruments. The approach includes requirement decomposition, flowdown, verification planning, and traceability within a configuration-controlled environment. We describe performance budgets for image quality, wavefront error, astrometry, and throughput, along with cross-instrument dependencies that require consistent modeling and disciplined change control. Examples illustrate reconciliation of science allocations with engineering estimates, resolution of interface issues, and the use of traceability tools. Finally, we recommend practices for multi-partner projects to reduce integration risk and support confidence in first-light performance.

Items.Authors: Pengfei Qiang, Lizhi Sheng, Yangji Yang
Items.Title: Research on key technology of soft X-ray focusing optical reflective coatings
Items.Abstract: Based on the eXTP satellite requirements, a Wolter-I focusing system was simulated with a 5250 mm focal length, 237 mm radius, 600 mm mirror length, and 45 layers. To optimize mirror coatings, the study examined surface roughness, mirror spacing, and materials using Monte Carlo simulations. Results show that dual-layer coatings, specifically Au+Ni4 and Au+C10, significantly enhance performance. With a mirror figure PV of 0.5 μm and RMS of 0.1 μm, the design achieved effective areas of 1000 cm² at 2 keV and 890 cm² at 6 keV. Furthermore, optimizing mirror spacing to 0.2 mm maximized the effective area while limiting stray light to below 4.8%.

Items.Authors: Mengmeng Qian, Jiahao Zhou, Wenfei Liu, Hongzhuan Hu, Jianping Wang, Zhigang Liu, Jiaru Chu, Ping Zhang, Zengxiang Zhou
Items.Title: Research on real-time simulation and control strategies for the LAMOST high-density fiber positioning control system
Items.Abstract: During the LAMOST telescope upgrade, the center-to-center spacing of fiber positioners has been reduced from 25.6 mm to 10.4 mm. Based on 4,000 focal-plane holes, 6,000–12,000 miniaturized positioners can be deployed. The original LAMOST control system supports only legacy 25.6 mm positioners and uses a single-threaded synchronous architecture, causing interface latency, delayed status synchronization, and limited exception handling in concurrent operation. To address these issues, this study develops a Qt-based simulation and control system with a layered architecture and an event-driven mechanism. Experiments show that the system displays the full focal-plane layout, maintains smooth interface response and reliable status synchronization during high-frequency multitasking, and identifies and avoids potential collision risks. The platform supports simulation verification, anomaly diagnosis, troubleshooting, and application for the LAMOST high-density fiber positioning system.

Items.Authors: J. M. Le Duigou, D. Bausch, N. Bray, C. A. Chevrier, M. Clavery, A. Courtois, F. Gant, B. Gorin, P. A. Goulm, C. Latry, G. Malbrancke, F. Mirc, A. Peus, D. Peyret, B. Regnier, H. Reininger, M. Sodki
Items.Title: Results of the DICOS ground tests
Items.Abstract: DICOS is a technological demonstrator under a stratospheric balloon for advanced pointing and wavefront stability technologies. The current funded phase of the project ended in december 2025 with a full scale ground demonstration of the telescope mounted on a testing stand. Combining measurements on an artificial star and on sky observations of Polaris, we demonstrate a rejection of 500 of the gondola residual wobbling, estimated to 10-20 arcsec at 0.5 Hz. The limiting factors are the structural first modes at 12 and 22 Hz and the 3 ms time delay in the fast pointing loop. The slow AO loop reaches 5 mn WFE with a stability better than 1 nm over 10 hours, on the optical bench only. Unfortunately, the 40 cm aluminum main mirror has important high spatial frequencies that prevent the phase diversity to perform well at instrument level.

Items.Authors: José San Juan, Rosario Cosentino, Luca Di Fabrizio, Marcos Hernández, Manuel González
Items.Title: Revamping the visible low resolution spectrograph of the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo: integrating legacy hardware into a modern web service architecture
Items.Abstract: The continuous operation of astronomical instrumentation, such as LRS at the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo (TNG), frequently faces the challenge of "asymmetric obsolescence": while optical components and CCD sensors retain their scientific validity, the associated control interfaces and computing environments become outdated. This work details the reverse engineering and software development required to migrate the detector control system to a modern computing infrastructure.

Items.Authors: H. Mahmoodzadeh, P. Saracco, I. Di Antonio, P. Conconi, D. Scaccabarozzi, B. Saggin, E. Molinari, C. Arcidiacono, I. Arosio, E. Cascone, V. Cianniello, Francesco D’Alessio, V. De Caprio, G. Di Rico, B. Di Francesco, C. Eredia, P. Franzetti, M. Fumana, E. Portaluri, Fabrizio Vitali
Items.Title: Review of the optomechanical design of SHARP: a near infrared spectrograph for the next generation telescope
Items.Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive overview of the last status of conceptual optomechanical design of SHARP, which has already been published as referenced paper in the Journal of Astronomical Telescopes, Instruments, and Systems (JATIS), including the optical architecture, mechanical structure, and key mechanisms developed to meet the demanding constraints imposed by the ELT environment. The optical design has been optimized to achieve high throughput and spectral performance while ensuring compactness and manufacturability under cryogenic and vacuum conditions.

Items.Authors: Tonya L. Peshel, Abigail Y. Pan, Tanmoy Chattopadhyay, Steven W. Allen, Marshall W. Bautz, Michael Cooper, Kevan Donlon, Catherine E. Grant, Sven Herrmann, Jill Juneau, Beverly J. LaMarr, Christopher Leitz, Adam B. Mantz, Eric D. Miller, R. Glenn Morris, Declan O'Neill, Peter Orel, Artem Poliszczuk, Gregory Prigozhin, Haley R. Stueber, Keith Warner
Items.Title: RNDR noise modeling in first-generation SiSeRO (Single-electron Sensitive Readout) devices
Items.Abstract: Flagship observatories require single-photon detectors with ultra-fast readout, sub-electron noise performance, and scalable large-format architectures. The X-ray Astronomy and Observational Cosmology group at Stanford, in collaboration with the MIT Kavli Institute and MIT Lincoln Laboratory, is developing readout technologies for next-generation charge-coupled devices (CCDs). Prototypes employing Single-electron Sensitive Readout (SiSeRO) amplifiers demonstrate excellent read noise and spectral performance using Repetitive Non-Destructive Readout (RNDR), achieving 0.5e- noise in under 50 cycles. We have modeled noise for longer RNDR cycles, exploring probabilistic mechanisms such as thermal leakage and impact ionization. Here we present our model results, including statistical limits on dark current-like signals. Maturation of SiSeRO technology will improve detector performance at soft X-ray energies, and addressing technology gaps for future X-ray, UV/optical and NIR observatories.

Items.Authors: HyeYun Park, Petr Kubánek, Kshitija Kelkar, Ignacio Sevilla-Noarbe, Andrea Jeremie, Brian Stalder, Bruno C. Quint, David Sanmartim, Dominique Boutigny, Douglas R. Neill, Erik Dennihy, Felipe Daruich, Freddy Muñoz Arancibia, Kevin Fanning, Kevin Reil, Laura Toribio San Cipriano, Malhar Sonaniskar, Marnia S. Pavlovic, Noah Gonzalez, Paulina Venegas, Sandrine Thomas, Tiago Ribeiro, Yijung Kang
Items.Title: Rubin M1M3 dynamic performance: stability and actuation during operations
Items.Abstract: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory is preparing to commence the Legacy Survey of Space and Time. Following integration of the complete Simonyi Survey Telescope, dynamic tests of the M1M3 primary/tertiary mirror assembly were conducted to verify operational readiness with respect to safety, stability, and image quality. The 8.4 m, 17 ton M1M3 system employs 156 force actuators and six hardpoint actuators to counteract gravitational and inertial loads while the telescope executes slews of order 1 degree per second even at 10 % of its speed, and must settle within 5 seconds between visits. Precisely coordinating the actuator forces under these high-speed motions is a significant control challenge. Test activities characterized hardpoint force control, assessed dynamical stability during slews and tracking, and evaluated force-actuator performance across a range of velocities and acceleration profiles consistent with the telescope’s expected operational envelope.

Items.Authors: Sergey Naroenkov, Evgeniy A. Kopylov, Michael Nalivkin, Mansur Ibragimov, Mikhail Sachkov, Sergey Potanin, Lidiya Bolbasova
Items.Title: Russian-Cuban observatory: instruments and astroclimate
Items.Abstract: It is reported that the first telescope of the Russian-Cuban Observatory, installed at the observatory's optical station in Havana, Republic of Cuba, has begun operation. The tasks for observations that are supposed to be carried out using the mentioned telescope are described. The Russian-Cuban integration scheme is described and some of its features are briefly discussed. It is reported that the astroclimate has been measured at selected sites in Cuba, where the next stage of the observatory's construction is expected to be implemented.

Items.Authors: Andrea Di Paola, Roberto Speziali, Maurizio Oliviero, Luciano Dal Sasso, Vincenzo Mauriello, Mauro Centrone
Items.Title: SAMM-E: the enhanced version of the solar activity magnetic monitor for the SAMM-NET space weather network
Items.Abstract: In June 2022, the first prototype of the SAMM (Solar Activity Magnetic Monitor) telescope was installed on the roof of the INAF-Monte Mario Astronomical Observatory in Rome, Italy, to test its capabilities for space weather observations. SAMM was designed to measure magnetic fields and Doppler velocities along the line of sight in the solar atmosphere at high cadence and two different heights. Building on the experience with the first prototype, an enhanced version of the SAMM telescope, SAMM-E, has been designed and built to overcome the limitations of its predecessor and provide a stable, reliable, and calibrated data source for space weather models. Here, we present the characteristics of the new instrument along with its first-light images, and discuss its planned use in the SAMM-NET network.

Items.Authors: Clémentine Béchet, Michel Tallon, Isabelle Tallon-Bosc, Éric Thiébaut, Isaac Dinis, Caroline Kulcsár, Henri-François Raynaud, Nicolas Galland, Markus Kasper, Florian Ferreira, Maud Langlois, Emiliano Diolaiti, Anthony Boccaletti
Items.Title: SAXO+, the second-stage adaptive optics for SPHERE: continuous learning of the temporal dynamics of the wavefront
Items.Abstract: SAXO+ is designed to reduce the temporal error of the AO correction compared to the existing AO in SPHERE today, by including a second stage of AO working at a higher frequency (up to 2.7kHz) and by controlling it with algorithms using predictive features. Among those, we present here an algorithm with the particular asset that its control components are continuously learned and updated at every loop. An affine direct temporal model of the incoming aberrations is learned during closed-loop AO observations. A generalization of the Recursive Least Squares algorithm is used to update on the fly this predictive model, without the need to invert any large matrix. This predictive model is combined with an iterative controller designed to account at every loop for possible spatial and temporal variations of the data precision. We show that the continuous learning of the temporal model improves the predictive AO correction when vibrations are modelized in SAXO+ numerical simulations.

Items.Authors: Paul Fontanillas, Florian Ferreira, Arnaud Sevin, Damien Gratatdour, Gaël Chauvin, Emiliano Diolaiti, Raffaele Gratton, Magali Loupias, Julien Milli, François Wildi, Anthony Boccaletti
Items.Title: SAXO+, the second-stage adaptive optics for SPHERE: RTC final design and performance results
Items.Abstract: SAXO+ is the upgrade of the SPHERE adaptive optics (AO) system. After passing its Final Design Review  in April 2025 it entered the Assembly, Integration and Testing (AIT) phase in April 2026, with first light  scheduled for 2028 on the VLT. This upgrade aims to enhance the SPHERE’s contrast performance. This  second stage will feature a pyramid wavefront sensor (PWFS) operating at high frame rates up to 3 kHz and  a deformable mirror (DM) with 952 actuators. In addition, SAXO+ will interface with the first stage  real-time controller (RTC), SPARTA. The SAXO+ RTC is based on the COSMIC platform for the hard real-  time layer and on the ESO RTC Toolkit for the soft real-time layer. Its modular design supports multiple  control strategies, including artificial intelligence (AI) approaches. This paper presents the final RTC architecture and the performance results.

Items.Authors: Isaac Dinis, Nicolas Galland, Henri-François Raynaud, Clémentine Béchet, Michel Tallon, Isabelle Tallon-Bosc, Maud Langlois, Florian Ferreira, François Wildi, Damien Ségransan, Anthony Boccaletti, Markus Kasper, Caroline Kulcsár
Items.Title: SAXO+, the second-stage adaptive optics for SPHERE: single vs cascade control loop performance assessment
Items.Abstract: This study compares two adaptive optics control architectures in the context of the SAXO+ instrument: the  cascade scheme, which is the SAXO+ baseline design, and a hypothetical single-loop scheme in which both  deformable mirrors (DMs) — the SAXO+ DM and SPHERE’s High-Order DM (HODM) — are jointly controlled  by the SAXO+ real-time computer (RTC) using solely the pyramid wavefront sensor (PWFS). All results are  obtained through end-to-end AO simulations performed with the COMPASS simulation platform. Results  demonstrate that when employing a first-order controller such as the Optimized Modal Gain Integrator (OMGI),  the cascade scheme outperforms the single-loop scheme by virtue of its double-rejection property. However, when  a predictive controller is applied, the single-loop scheme achieves comparable performance to the cascade scheme,  while considerably reducing control complexity by eliminating the need for dual-stage tuning.

Items.Authors: Mario Castro, Alvaro Quintana, Jorge Parra
Items.Title: SCADA system development for multiple telescopes employing a distributed and standardized architecture
Items.Abstract: .With the objective of increasing operational efficiency, the National Optical-Infrared Astronomy Research Laboratory (NOIRLab) is implementing tools that aim to optimize resource usage, downtime, maintenance strategies and gather useful data for smart decision-making. In this context NOIRLab will deploy a Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) for monitoring and controlling support systems for its main seven telescopes, including Vera C.Rubin. These systems will require data logging, plot historical and real time data, generate reports and alarm management.  NOIRLab’s approach is presented in order to create a reusable SCADA application across seven sites, including common software layer definitions, taxonomy-based tag tree construction and the use of standards and best practices for symbology, alarm configuration, and human machine interfaces. It is also shown the recommended server architecture that guarantees robustness, backup availability and interoperability across site

Items.Authors: Hans-Joachim Hess, Sriparsann S. Annadevara, Helmut Kravcar, Sebastian Steuer, Naman Pujari, Ralf Bender
Items.Title: Scaling PLC control systems for the MICADO cryostat: implementation and challenges
Items.Abstract: MICADO, the first-light instrument for the ESO Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), is currently in the integration and test phase of the project, with expected first light in 2030.  In large instrumentation projects the demand on sensors and actuators is often creating space issues for the control electronics. Considering this with respect to the MICADO cryostat, as well as its demanding cryogenic, operational, and integration requirements, we created a dedicated cryostat control system. A solution will be described for specific heater PCBs in conjunction with the traditional Beckhoff PLC system to ensure electromagnetic robustness for sensitive channel under all operational environmental conditions.  The selection process for off the-the-shelve PLC systems, the choice of terminals and the integration into a single instrument control system (ICS) is described in more detail for the ICS01 cryogenic-vacuum control cabinet, explaining the maintenance friendly cabling and repair concept.

Items.Authors: John Rankin, Stefano Basso, Sergio Campana, Marta Civitani, Paolo Conconi, Vincenzo Cotroneo, Giovanni Pareschi, Daniele Spiga
Items.Title: Searching for gravitational wave events counterparts in x-rays by tilting the multiple shells of Wolter-I optics
Items.Abstract: Current X-ray telescopes have a combination of field of view and angular resolution unsuitable to accurately localize the electromagnetic counterparts of gravitational wave events. This will become increasingly important when the LIGO and Virgo experiments will work at full sensitivity, when the Einstein Telescope observatory will come online, or with the space mission LISA, all in the next decade. With the goal of having a source localization accuracy of tens of arcsec over a ~10 square degrees field of view, together with hundreds of cm^2 effective area, we study how Wolter-I optics can be appropriately modified. We compare the advantages and drawbacks of each optical design, in particular regarding the contribution of stray light.

Items.Authors: Fabrice Pancher, Sébastien Soler, Fabien Malbet, Hugo Rousset, Manon Lizzana, Alain Léger, Thierry Lépine, Florence Ardellier-Desages, Jérôme Amiaux, Pierre-Olivier Lagage
Items.Title: Setup and performance of focal-plane characterization benches for high-precision astrometry
Items.Abstract: Detecting Earth-like exoplanets requires micro-arcsecond astrometry, which relies on a precisely calibrated focal plane equipped with high-resolution detectors. Accurate calibration depends on characterizing detector imperfections and systematic effects. Optical benches have been developed to assess the sensor’s behavior: an integrating-sphere setup for electro-optical parameters, an interferometric bench for pixel-level geometry, and a star-field projection system for intrinsic distortion. This work presents the characterization benches built for a 46-MP imaging sensor, based on the same technology as the four 220-MP detectors foreseen for the final focal-plane, and the performance metrics obtained from these setups in the context of NASA’s HWO and ESA’s M-class missions. Upgrades will bring the test environment closer to operational conditions: a second 46-MP sensor will be added for multi-detector tests, plus an adjustable-angle fringe-projection system and improved alignment.

Items.Authors: Tristen M. Sextro, Randall L. McEntaffer, Nicolas M. Barrière, Ramses Günther, David Girou
Items.Title: Silicon pore optics spectrograph architecture for future explorer-class soft x-ray missions
Items.Abstract: Future soft X-ray astronomy missions require compact, lightweight spectrographs capable of high spectral resolution within mass and volume limits of explorer-class spacecraft. Silicon Pore Optics (SPO) developed by cosine and ESA have emerged as a leading technology for X-ray telescopes for their low mass, high stiffness, and modular fabrication. This work investigates an SPO-based spectrograph concept where primary focusing optics and diffraction elements are made using SPO manufacturing techniques. By engineer-matching focal length, pore geometry, and alignment tolerances between mirror and grating, a system can be optimized as a unified instrument rather than a combination of independent components. The design will be evaluated with ray-tracing simulations to assess resolving power, throughput, and sensitivity to alignment errors. This approach aims to pioneer the SPO mirror + SPO grating architecture as a path toward future spectroscopy-dedicated missions in X-ray astronomy.

Items.Authors: Alexis Lau, A. J. Eldorado Riggs, Susan Redmond, Eric J. Cady, John E. Krist, Iva Laginja, Dan Sirbu, Lukas Delaye, Rémi Soummer, Sophie Noiret, Jean-Charles Lambert, Alexis Bidot
Items.Title: Simulation tools for realistic high-order wavefront correction with the Roman Coronagraph
Items.Abstract: NASA's Roman Space Telescope carries the Coronagraph Instrument to perform the first high-contrast imaging of exoplanets in space. The instrument’s only top-level requirement is to demonstrate a broadband dark zone. The Community Participation Program (CPP) is planning a range of scientific and engineering activities to perform afterward. To provide realistic simulations of Roman Coronagraph performance in these various modes, the CPP’s Hardware Working Group is developing the corgihowfsc software package. This repository is a wrapper combining several other repositories open-sourced by the Roman Coronagraph project and CPP: corgisim for producing realistic images, cgi-howfsc for performing and high-order wavefront sensing and control (HOWFSC), cgi-eetc for exposure time calculation, and cgi-coralign for performing optical calibrations. By using this collection of official modeling tools, the modeling results from the CPP will be the highest possible fidelity.

Items.Authors: Luca Cortese, Giuseppe Viterbo, Carmelo Arcidiacono, Matteo Simioni, Fabio Rossi, Alessio Turchi, Alfio Puglisi, Guido Agapito, Daniele Vassallo, Lorenzo Merli, Elena Masciadri, Enrico Pinna, Francesco Maio, Davide Fedele, Arseniy Kuznetsov
Items.Title: Simulation-based inference of atmospheric parameters from adaptive optics telemetry data
Items.Abstract: Inferring atmospheric parameters for observational astronomy is important for different reasons, such as the evaluation and characterization of astronomical sites and point spread function estimation.  This could be performed by exploiting telemetry data saved by Adaptive Optics (AO) systems. The retrieval of parameters such as horizontal wind speed, wind direction, and integrated turbulence quantities from these data is a challenging task, also due to intrinsic degeneracies.  In order to face this problem, we aim to perform amortized Bayesian posterior estimation with a Simulation-Based Inference approach (SBI). This method makes use of Neural Networks (NNs) as density estimators. The dataset used to train the model is generated with the end-to-end AO simulator SPECULA.   This method provides sub-second inference and could be adapted to real data via fine-tuning.

Items.Authors: Mary Kreidel, Byeongho Eom, Henry LeDuc, Peter Day
Items.Title: Simulations of aluminum resonant absorbers for energy-resolving mid-IR MKIDs
Items.Abstract: Mid-infrared detectors with high sensitivity and stability are essential for spectroscopic and interferometric studies of exoplanets orbiting nearby stars. Spectroscopic detectors can monitor star-exoplanet systems for transit and phase curve variations, and in interferometric applications, starlight is suppressed to enable individual photon detection. Kinetic inductance detector (KID) arrays developed for the far-infrared (240–25 µm) have recently set new benchmarks in both performance aspects, utilizing a resonant absorber design that allows otherwise highly-reflective aluminum to become about 75% absorptive at the targeted frequency[1]. Here, we discuss the design of KID arrays for the mid-infrared band (20–4 µm). We describe simulations of resonant absorbers for that wavelength that take into account high frequency effects, such as reduced skin depth. We predict the performance of our designs in the mid-infrared by scaling our results at 25 µm.  [1] Phys. Rev. X 14, 041005 (2024)

Items.Authors: Matteo Di Carlo, Ugur Yilmaz, Mauro Dolci
Items.Title: SKA-Tango-Exporter: a diagnostic tool for analysing interrelated problems in the TANGO-controls environment, tailored to the needs of the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) project
Items.Abstract: The ska-tango-exporter is a diagnostic tool designed to extract comprehensive information from a TANGO-controls–based system deployed in a Kubernetes cluster (within a continuous integration/continuous deployment – CI/CD context). Its purpose is to support the analysis of complex, interconnected problems that are often difficult to manage with standard tools.  It leverages existing data sources such as the TANGO database and Kubernetes’ etcd, together with internal monitoring systems including Prometheus (for attribute collection in a polling fashion) and InfluxDB (for event tracking). Starting from TANGO v10, the exporter can also enable OpenTelemetry metrics, providing a standardized way to integrate with modern observability platforms and extend monitoring capabilities.

Items.Authors: Yiqiao Yang, Xiaoyan Li, Jiajia Wu
Items.Title: Slit-referenced auto-guiding system for the spectrograph of the SiTian Pilot-Node Telescope
Items.Abstract: As a pilot node of the SiTian Project,the Wuhan University 1 m telescope is equipped with a low-resolution spectrograph. During long-duration spectroscopic observations, mechanical factors and environmental disturbances cause stellar image drift. This study discusses an auto-guiding system with a slit designed to compensate for this drift. The key techniques include image preprocessing, slit edge detection, star centroid extraction, and real-time axes decoupling. Specifically, the system employs a dual-channel feature decoupling algorithm to identify the slits and target stars. Furthermore, it addresses the nonlinear coupling of the control axes by constructing a coordinate transformation matrix based on the real-time parallactic angle.The experimental results demonstrate that the system stabilizes the target star within the 1 arcsecond slit, achieving a centroiding accuracy better than 0.01 pixels and an average processing time of less than 10 ms.

Items.Authors: Federico Battaini, Pietro Schipani, Kalyan Radhakrishnan, Mirko Colapietro, Simone Di Filippo, Riccardo Claudi, Matteo Aliverti, Davide Ricci, Silvio Di Rosa, Matteo Munari, Sergio D'Orsi, Fabrizio Vitali, Matteo Genoni, David Young, José Antonio Araiza-Durán, Sergio Campana, Francesco D'Alessio, Rosario Cosentino, Paolo D'Avanzo, Salvatore Scuderi, Lorenzo Cabona, Laura Asquini, Sagi Ben-Ami, Ofir Hershko, Anna Brucalassi, Ricardo Zanmar Sanchez, Giuliano Pignata, Marco Landoni, Jani Achrén, Andrea Baruffolo, Alex Bichkovsky, Federico Biondi, Giulio Capasso, Enrico Cappellaro, Massimo Della Valle, Rosario Di Benedetto, Luigi Lessio, Gianluca Li Causi, Adam Rubin, Maximilian Stritzinger, Bernardo Salasnich, Stephen Smartt, Hector Pérez Ventura, Marco Riva, Seppo Mattila, Laurent Marty
Items.Title: SOXS at NTT: results and lesson learned during the preliminary acceptance in Europe phase from an AIV perspective
Items.Abstract: The Son Of X-Shooter (SOXS) is the dedicated spectroscopic follow-up facility for transient astronomy at the ESO NTT, providing simultaneous coverage from 350 nm to 2000 nm with an average resolving power of R∼4500 for a 1″ slit.  Following the successful completion of the Preliminary Acceptance in Europe (PAE) in late 2024, we assessed the instrument performance through a comprehensive verification campaign, including spectroscopic characterization, flexure compensation, cryogenic validation, detector and calibration-unit testing, and end-to-end operational checks.  We present the main results of these activities, summarize the corrective actions implemented after acceptance, and discuss the key lessons learned for future ESO instrumentation projects and for the ongoing commissioning phase at the telescope.

Items.Authors: Laura Schreiber, Emiliano Diolaiti, Davide Ricci, Andrea La Camera, Marcello Ravenna, Giuliana Fiorentino, Carmela Lardo, Claudia Mignone, Maria Tantalo, Antonino Nunnari, Vittorio Francesco Braga
Items.HTMLTitle: Starfinder: from IDL to open-source Python TM software for empirical PSF modeling and crowded-field analysis in high-resolution imaging
Items.Title: Starfinder: from IDL to open-source Python software for empirical PSF modeling and crowded-field analysis in high-resolution imaging
Items.Abstract: We present the final Python release of the Starfinder crowded-field photometry/astrometry package for images with complex, spatially variable PSFs, especially from adaptive optics. The code retains the proven empirical-PSF methodology while adding a modern GUI built on a client–server concept and performance/functional upgrades. New optimizations target very large images and extended PSF models, enabling efficient analysis of future ELT-scale datasets. Starfinder is instrument-agnostic, suitable for AO imaging as well as diffraction-limited space data, and is released open access with documentation and tutorials.

Items.Authors: Melissa Flores, Alexa LaPinta, Caden Burkhardt, John D. Monnier, James Cutler, Leonid Pogorelyuk
Items.Title: STARI fiber-injection prototype testing and simulation
Items.Abstract: The STarlight Acquisition and Reflection toward Interferometry (STARI) is a NASA-funded joint mission to advance technology for future space interferometry with two 8U cubeSATs to collect/transfer starlight between each other using a single mode fiber. We present a lab proof-of-concept for a two satellite system demonstrating fiber-coupling and simulations for starlight transmission between satellites.The first payload is the Pupil Transport (PT) that collects the incoming starlight and reflects it into the other spacecraft. The second is the Fiber Injection and Detection (FID) that injects the reflected starlight into a single-mode fiber on the other spacecraft and uses itself as a referenceIn this lab set-up, we achieve a 90.9% match to the simulation results for optimal coupling efficiency. This level of coupling efficiency can then be used in future missions to collect meteorology data on stars and exoplanets using formation flying fiber coupled systems.
